title: Some law profs move to old-school assessment methods to combat AI
author: Julianne Hill

dom.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source accepts that AI use or polished output does not establish independent legal judgment and materially develops the cluster’s proposition with concrete assessment designs—especially oral follow-up, supervised testing and experiential work—that require students to demonstrate and defend their reasoning while AI remains part of instruction. Its reported benefits are instructor observations rather than comparative evidence of durable competence.

kp.k: AI complicates assessment of students’ independent legal reasoning
kp.d: The article reports that some law professors are returning to oral exams, handwritten tests and locked-down software to distinguish students’ own knowledge from AI-assisted performance. Stetson professor Kirsten K. Davis says many professors have reduced outside-class writing assignments because AI can produce passable novice-level work. These are reported teaching experiences and concerns, not findings from a systematic study.
qs: “One of the core questions for legal education is how do you adapt to the presence of a tool that can mimic or mask what looks like analysis?” says Kirsten K. Davis, a professor at Stetson Law.
“The worry you have is that a test will not tell you what a student knows.”

Many professors already have ditched or cut back on writing assignments outside of class “because AI can do a fairly decent job of replicating what a novice can do in a way that’s passable,” she adds.

kp.k: Oral questioning tests students’ ability to defend legal analysis
kp.d: Quinnipiac professor Wayne Unger uses one-on-one, 30-minute oral exam appointments in smaller classes and handwritten exams in larger courses. The oral final accounts for 50% of the grade; students receive the prompt and grading criteria about a week ahead and may bring notes. Appointments comprise 20 minutes of testing and 10 minutes of feedback. Unger argues that probing follow-up questions expose whether students understand and can defend their analysis, including when AI assisted preparation.
qs: In his larger courses, he switched to “pen-and-paper only,” with all responses handwritten.
In Unger’s smaller classes, the final oral exam is 50% of the grade, so “they have to take it seriously,” he says.
Students schedule their exam appointment, which includes 20 minutes for the test and 10 minutes of feedback.
“If they can’t defend it, if they can’t go deeper into the analysis, then it shows.”

kp.k: Independent thinking remains a professional formation objective
kp.d: Unger presents AI-restricted assessment as a way to develop critical thinking, analogical reasoning and thinking on one’s feet rather than letting technology perform those activities. Davis similarly argues that students need sustained critical engagement and their own legal intelligence to use AI. The article also invokes professional competence as requiring lawyers to read and understand potentially relevant material.
qs: “I want to develop a skill set with our students—that’s critical thinking, that’s analogical reasoning, that’s on-your-feet thinking,” Unger says, “and I can’t do that if a tech solution does all that for them.”
“Our basic rules of professional responsibility say you must be competent in your practice, and that means if you discover something that might be relevant, you need to read it and understand it.”
“The three words that I use are ‘sustained critical engagement.’ How do I keep them active on the project when I’m not there?” Stetson’s Davis says.
“My mantra has been, ‘You must have lawyer intelligence to use artificial intelligence.’ ”

kp.k: Unger reports positive feedback and reduced post-exam grading
kp.d: Unger says students appreciate immediate feedback and that even relatively poor performers supported oral assessment because it lets them demonstrate skills beyond standardized testing. He also reports avoiding two weeks of post-exam grading and feeling more confident in students’ knowledge than when assessing papers. These are his observations, without quantified comparative outcome evidence.
qs: “Even the students who have performed relatively poorly still very much enjoyed and supported this form of assessment,” he says.
“It allows them to display other skills than on the standardized test model.”
“I’m not spending two weeks after the exam grading,” he adds, “and I’m more confident that the students know the material than when they turn in papers.”

kp.k: Schools adopt differing restrictions and supervised assessment policies
kp.d: The article reports that Berkeley Law banned AI for class assignments and exams in May, while Texas Law Dean Robert “Bobby” Chesney called earlier in the month of publication for Socratic-style questioning and treating classroom time as the context for certainty about unaided learning. Case Western Dean Paul Rose describes in-person final exams with hard-copy-only access and encourages verbal components for paper-heavy grading or staged writing to observe progress. These institutional approaches coexist with the article’s statement that all professors it contacted intentionally use AI in teaching and assignments.
qs: None of the professors contacted by the ABA Journal ban AI, and all purposefully and intentionally use it in their classrooms and assignments.

In May, the University of California at Berkeley School of Law [banned](https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/uc-berkeley-law-school-restricts-use-of-ai-by-students) students from using artificial intelligence for class assignments and during exams.

At Case Western University School of Law, Dean Paul Rose notes “the default rule is that final exams are administered in person and are either closed-book or open-book with access only to hard-copy materials and no access to digital copies, computer hard drives or the internet.”

“We also encourage faculty to include a verbal component if a significant portion of the grade for a course is based on a paper or to do writing assignments in stages so faculty can observe students’ progress over time,” he adds.

kp.k: Writing instruction combines AI access with process-based safeguards
kp.d: Northwestern’s AI and Legal Education Committee recommends considering multiple approaches rather than a single prohibition: broad AI use, AI tutors throughout writing projects, oral assessment, disclosure of AI use, or restrictions to particular writing stages. North Carolina Central’s April Dawson supports these options and recommends more presentations, simulations and client conversations to develop professional skills.
qs: Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law’s AI and Legal Education Committee advises faculty to identify challenges in writing courses and suggests considering a variety of approaches, like allowing broad AI use, providing AI tutors at each stage of writing projects, and including an oral assessment, says Daniel W. Linna, director of law and technology initiatives.
Northwestern instructors can consider whether students must disclose how AI was used or only allow AI only at early or later stages of the writing process, he adds.
“Changing how we assess is necessary.”

Dawson notes the need to also rethink the structure of class time, incorporating more experiential learning— such as presentations, simulations and client conversations—to develop professional skills in the age of AI.

kp.k: Locked-down testing replaces one professor’s final writing assignment
kp.d: Stetson professor Linda Anderson replaced a substantial end-of-semester memo or appellate brief in Research & Writing with an in-class test on locked-down software because she did not want uncertainty about AI authorship. The test combines performance tests, multiple-choice questions and short answers, modeled on the NextGen UBE Bar Exam, whose first administration the 2026 article says is scheduled for July. Anderson explicitly states that AI helped her build the test.
qs: “I didn’t want to find myself in a situation where I couldn’t tell whether it was AI-generated or not,” Anderson says.
Instead of the typical end-of-semester writing assignment, like a big office memo or appellate brief, she moved to an in-class test conducted on locked-down software.
The test’s format, including performance tests, multiple-choice questions and short answers, is based on the NextGen UBE Bar Exam, which set to have its first administration in July.
“AI helped me build the test. I’ll be very clear about that,” she says.

kp.k: Linna warns against overcorrecting toward AI avoidance
kp.d: Northwestern’s Daniel W. Linna accepts that assessment adjustments may help but warns against using them primarily to avoid AI. He recommends redesigning courses around learning objectives and using AI tutors, mentors and simulations to accelerate learning and skill development. This is a recommendation, not a demonstrated learning-effect finding; the article concludes that approaches must be course-specific.
qs: “Adjustments to assessments may be useful, but they’re being implemented to avoid AI when we need to embrace it,” he says.

“Professors need to be proactive, consider the learning objectives of their courses, and redesign them to make the most of AI to accelerate student learning and skill development” via AI tutors, mentors and simulations.
All agree there is no set formula for AI use, and each course demands specific consideration.
“Faculty need to get engaged and figure out what is best for their courses to ensure that students are achieving the learning outcomes,” Linna says.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI is changing legal education by making students’ independent reasoning harder to assess, prompting some professors to restore oral, handwritten and controlled in-class examinations; interviewees also argue for intentional AI-assisted learning.
pts.d: Julianne Hill reports changes to assessment practices rather than predictions about legal-service markets or lawyer employment. Kirsten K. Davis claims AI can produce passable novice-level writing and can mask whether students understand the material, leading many professors to reduce out-of-class writing assignments. Wayne Unger argues that outsourcing thinking to technology undermines the development of critical thinking, analogical reasoning and spontaneous reasoning. He says probing oral examinations expose students’ inability to defend or deepen an analysis, increase his confidence in their knowledge and avoid weeks of subsequent grading. Linda Anderson reports replacing a major end-of-semester writing assignment with a locked-down in-class test because she could not confidently distinguish students’ work from AI-generated work; she also used AI to construct that test. April Dawson argues that assessment and class structure must change, including more experiential learning. Daniel W. Linna cautions against an avoidance-focused response and advocates redesigning courses around AI tutors, mentors and simulations to accelerate learning and skill development. This proposed learning benefit is presented as an advocated opportunity, not a measured outcome.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of interviewees’ teaching experience and concrete institutional practices; the article supplies no quantitative assessment of AI’s effects on learning or assessment validity.
pts.d: Unger describes his own oral examinations, handwritten examinations, immediate feedback and students’ reported acceptance of the oral format. Anderson describes her first controlled test in a Research & Writing course she has taught for about 20 years. These are practitioner accounts, not comparative studies establishing learning gains or reliable identification of AI dependence. Dean Paul Rose describes Case Western’s default in-person examination rules and encouragement of verbal components or staged writing. Linna describes Northwestern’s committee guidance, which includes broad AI use, AI tutors, oral assessment and possible disclosure or stage-specific restrictions. Hill also reports Berkeley restrictions and a University of Texas dean’s call for Socratic questioning as examples of institutional responses, not evidence that those responses improve outcomes. Davis’s claim about AI’s novice-writing capability and Linna’s proposed acceleration of learning are not supported here by benchmarks, datasets or measured results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes changes already occurring at the time of its 2026 publication, with course-specific conditions rather than a universal policy or dated forecast.
pts.d: Unger uses individual oral examinations in smaller classes and handwritten responses in larger courses. His oral final constitutes 50% of the grade; students receive the prompt and grading criteria about a week beforehand, may bring notes, and receive 20 minutes of questioning followed by 10 minutes of feedback. His claimed ability to expose weak understanding depends on follow-up questioning, not simply on whether AI was used in preparation. Anderson’s change is described as recent, with a format modeled on the NextGen UBE, whose first administration the article places in July. Hill dates Berkeley’s restriction to 'In May' and the Texas dean’s call to 'Earlier this month'; the supplied text does not establish the precise publication date needed to resolve those references. None of the interviewed professors bans AI outright: restrictions apply to particular assessments alongside deliberate classroom and assignment use. Linna’s learning-acceleration argument is conditional on proactive redesign around course objectives, with no specified horizon for results.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are law students, professors and law-school administrators, with professional competence supplying the longer-term rationale.
pts.d: Students face less reliance on take-home writing, more live demonstrations of understanding and, in some settings, restricted access to digital materials. Unger reports that oral assessment lets students demonstrate skills beyond standardized testing and receive immediate feedback. Students may also receive AI-assisted tutoring and simulation-based instruction under the approaches discussed. Professors must redesign assessment and instruction, balance AI use against independent skill development, and manage individual examination appointments; Unger reports reduced post-exam grading time. Schools and their committees must set defaults while allowing course-specific choices. Davis and Unger connect these educational changes to future lawyers’ ability to reason and understand relevant material independently. The article does not claim measured downstream effects on clients, legal fees, law-firm staffing or access to justice.
